objectives: Distinguish effusive lava emplacement (pāhoehoe vs ʻaʻā) and the controls on flow morphology.
Describe explosive eruption products: tephra grain sizes, pyroclastic density currents, and lahars.
Explain the structure and dynamics of an eruption column, including the convective and umbrella regions.

slides.title: Effusive eruptions: pāhoehoe and ʻaʻā
slides.body:
When low-viscosity, gas-poor magma reaches the surface, it does not explode — it flows. **Effusive** eruptions produce **lava flows**, and the two classic surface textures of basaltic flows carry **Hawaiian** names that volcanology adopted worldwide: **pāhoehoe** and **ʻaʻā**.

**Pāhoehoe** (pronounced pah-HOH-ee-hoh-ee) is smooth, billowy, and ropy. It forms when fluid, hotter, slower-shearing lava develops a flexible glassy skin that wrinkles into rope-like folds as the still-molten interior drags beneath it. Pāhoehoe advances by inflating and sending out shiny **toes** and **lobes**, and it often roofs over to form **lava tubes** — insulated conduits that let lava travel many kilometers with little heat loss, as seen on **Kīlauea** and **Mauna Loa** in Hawaii.

**ʻAʻā** (pronounced AH-ah) is rough, clinkery, and rubbly, a jagged surface of broken fragments called **clinker** that is genuinely painful to walk on. It forms when the same kind of lava is **cooler**, **more degassed**, **more viscous**, or sheared faster, so that the crust repeatedly breaks rather than folds. A single flow can transition from pāhoehoe to ʻaʻā downslope as it cools and degasses; the reverse rarely happens.

The physics dividing the two is **strain rate versus viscosity**. At a given viscosity, slow flow yields pāhoehoe and fast flow yields ʻaʻā; at a given strain rate, low viscosity yields pāhoehoe and high viscosity yields ʻaʻā. The crossover is captured well by simple flow models. A basic estimate of the average velocity $\bar{u}$ of a Newtonian lava sheet of thickness $h$ on a slope $\theta$ is the **Jeffreys equation**,

$$ \bar{u} = \frac{\rho\, g\, h^2 \sin\theta}{3\,\eta} $$

so thicker, steeper, less viscous flows move faster — and faster shear pushes the surface toward ʻaʻā. More viscous compositions go further still: **andesite** and **dacite** are too stiff to flow far and instead pile up around the vent as steep-sided **lava domes** (such as the dacite dome that grew in the crater of **Mount St. Helens** after 1980) or thick, slow **block lava** flows with angular blocky surfaces. The most extreme silicic flows barely move at all. Thus even within purely effusive activity, the silica-viscosity control of the earlier lessons reappears: it sets not only whether a volcano flows or explodes, but the very texture of the rock it leaves behind.

question.question: A basaltic lava flow starts out smooth and ropy near the vent but becomes rough and clinkery farther downslope. What most likely caused the change from pāhoehoe to ʻaʻā?
options: The lava became hotter and less viscous downslope
The lava cooled and degassed as it traveled, raising its viscosity and increasing surface shear so the crust broke instead of folding
The composition changed from basalt to rhyolite within a few hundred meters
Rain fell on the flow and roughened its surface
question.explanation: Pāhoehoe forms from hotter, more fluid, slowly sheared lava whose skin folds into ropes. As a flow travels it loses heat and gas, raising viscosity; the crust then fractures into clinker rather than folding, producing ʻaʻā. The pāhoehoe-to-ʻaʻā transition downslope is common and essentially one-way; the reverse is rare.

hints: What happens to temperature and gas content as lava travels?
Pāhoehoe folds; ʻaʻā breaks. What favors breaking?
slides.workedSolution: Travel cools and degasses the lava, which raises its viscosity. Higher viscosity (and the higher shear of a thinning, advancing flow) causes the crust to fracture into jagged clinker rather than fold into ropes, so pāhoehoe transitions to ʻaʻā downslope. The composition does not change; option B is correct.

slides.title: Explosive products: tephra, PDCs, and lahars
slides.body:
When viscous, gas-rich magma fragments, the eruption ejects shattered material collectively called **tephra** (or **pyroclasts**, meaning 'fire-broken'). Geologists sort tephra by grain size on a logarithmic scale:
- **Ash** — fragments smaller than **2 mm**. Fine ash is microscopic shards of volcanic glass; it travels farthest, abrades engines and lungs, collapses roofs under its weight, and grounds aircraft (as **Eyjafjallajökull** did across Europe in 2010).
- **Lapilli** — fragments **2–64 mm** (Italian for 'little stones').
- **Blocks and bombs** — fragments larger than **64 mm**. **Blocks** are angular, ejected solid; **bombs** are ejected molten and aerodynamically shaped in flight (spindle, ribbon, and breadcrust bombs).

A particularly important product is **pumice**, a frothy, glassy rock so full of frozen gas bubbles (vesicles) that it can float on water — the solidified foam of an explosive eruption. Its dense, dark counterpart from basaltic fire fountains is **scoria** (or **cinder**).

The deadliest explosive phenomenon is the **pyroclastic density current (PDC)** — a ground-hugging avalanche of hot gas, ash, and rock that races downslope at up to several hundred kilometers per hour and temperatures of hundreds of degrees Celsius. Its more dilute, turbulent variety is a **pyroclastic surge**; its dense, concentrated variety is a **pyroclastic flow** or, in the older French term, a **nuée ardente**. It was a PDC from **Mont Pelée** that obliterated **Saint-Pierre** in **1902**, and PDCs from **Vesuvius** in **79 AD** that entombed **Herculaneum** and **Pompeii**. PDCs outrun people and cannot be escaped on foot; avoidance through evacuation is the only defense.

A second, slower, but far-reaching killer is the **lahar** — an Indonesian term for a volcanic mudflow or debris flow, a slurry of ash and water with the consistency of wet concrete that follows river valleys for tens of kilometers. Lahars form when eruptions melt summit snow and ice, when rain remobilizes loose ash, or when a crater lake breaks out. The **1985** eruption of **Nevado del Ruiz** in Colombia was small (VEI 3), yet its lahars buried the town of **Armero** and killed roughly **23,000** people — a stark reminder that secondary products, not just the blast, define volcanic risk. Together tephra, PDCs, and lahars form the explosive product suite that the silica-rich magmas of subduction zones routinely produce, and they are the focus of the hazard and monitoring work in the next lesson.

question.question: A volcanic fragment measures **30 mm** across. Using the standard tephra grain-size classes (ash < 2 mm; lapilli 2-64 mm; blocks/bombs > 64 mm), which size class does it belong to? Answer with the class name.
question.hint: 30 mm falls between 2 mm and 64 mm.

slides.title: The anatomy of an eruption column
slides.body:
The towering plume that **Pliny the Younger** likened to a pine tree is a true fluid-dynamical structure, and understanding it is central to forecasting ashfall and recognizing when a column will collapse into deadly PDCs. A sustained explosive eruption drives a vertical **eruption column** that has three distinct regions stacked from the vent upward.

**1. The gas-thrust region** (lowest, a few hundred meters to ~1 km). Here the erupting mixture of gas and pyroclasts is denser than the surrounding air and is propelled upward purely by its **momentum** as it is jetted from the vent at velocities that can exceed 100–600 m/s. The mixture decelerates rapidly as gravity acts on it.

**2. The convective region** (the bulk of the column, often the great majority of its height). As the rising jet **entrains** and heats cool ambient air, that air expands and the bulk mixture becomes **less dense than the atmosphere**. The column now rises by **buoyancy**, like a giant thermal, and this is what carries ash to great altitude. The maximum height $H$ of the convective column scales with the eruption's thermal power: a widely used relation is approximately

$$ H \approx 0.22\, \dot{Q}^{1/4} $$

(in SI units, with $\dot{Q}$ the heat-release rate), so column height grows only as the *fourth root* of eruption intensity — which is why even an order-of-magnitude increase in eruption rate raises the plume modestly. Large eruptions can punch columns **30–40 km** high, well into the **stratosphere**.

**3. The umbrella region** (the top, the 'branches' of Pliny's pine tree). When the buoyant column reaches its **level of neutral buoyancy** — the altitude where it matches the density of the stratified atmosphere — it can rise no farther and spreads laterally as an **umbrella cloud**, drifting downwind to deposit a fan of **tephra fall**.

The single most dangerous transition is **column collapse**. If the eruption ejects too much dense material too fast, or contains too little gas to entrain enough air, the mixture never becomes buoyant; the gas-thrust jet fountains up and falls back, and the collapsing mass spreads outward as a **pyroclastic density current**. Many of history's lethal PDCs were generated this way. Whether a column rises to the stratosphere or collapses into a killing ground current depends on the mass eruption rate, the gas content, and the vent geometry — a knife-edge that volcanologists model carefully. Reading a column's behavior in real time, from its height and stability, is one of the most important skills in eruption response, and it ties directly to the hazards and monitoring tools we examine next.

question.question: An eruption column is rising steadily and reaches the stratosphere, then spreads sideways into a broad umbrella cloud. What drives the column upward through most of its height, and why does it stop rising at the umbrella level?
options: Momentum from the vent carries it the whole way; it stops when the vent stops erupting
Buoyancy, after the column entrains and heats air to become less dense than the atmosphere; it stops at the level of neutral buoyancy where its density matches the surroundings
Wind pushes it up and then sideways
Magnetic forces lift the ash and then release it
question.explanation: Above the brief gas-thrust (momentum) region, the column entrains and heats ambient air, becoming less dense than the atmosphere, so it rises by buoyancy like a giant thermal. It can rise only until it reaches the level of neutral buoyancy, where its density equals that of the stratified atmosphere; there it spreads laterally as an umbrella cloud.

hints: Most of the column's rise is convective, not from momentum.
Spreading happens where the plume can no longer rise because densities match.
slides.workedSolution: The gas-thrust region is brief; thereafter the column entrains air, heats it, and becomes buoyant, rising convectively to great altitude. Rise ceases at the level of neutral buoyancy, where the plume density equals the ambient atmospheric density, and the cloud spreads laterally into an umbrella. Option B captures both the driving mechanism and the stopping condition.

question.question: Reading the products to reconstruct an eruption
question.prompt: Geologists mapping a stratovolcano find, from bottom to top: a thick basal layer of well-sorted pumice lapilli fall, then a chaotic, poorly sorted deposit of ash and blocks that drapes valleys and thins over ridges, and finally a sheet of mud-rich debris filling a river valley downstream. Interpret each of these three deposits in terms of eruptive process (tephra fall, pyroclastic density current, or lahar), and explain what the change from the first layer to the second layer implies about the behavior of the eruption column.

slides.title: From style to consequence
slides.body:
Eruption style is the bridge between a volcano's chemistry and its consequences for the world around it. This lesson has traced that bridge in both directions.

At the **effusive** end, low-viscosity basalt from places like **Kīlauea** and **Iceland** produces lava flows whose very texture records their conditions. **Pāhoehoe** marks hotter, slower, gas-rich emplacement and builds insulating **lava tubes**; **ʻaʻā** marks cooler, faster-sheared, degassed flow; and stiffer **andesite** and **dacite** scarcely flow at all, piling into **lava domes** and **block flows**. The **Jeffreys equation** for flow velocity makes the controls explicit — thickness, slope, and inverse viscosity.

At the **explosive** end, viscous gas-rich magma fragments into **tephra**, sorted from **ash** (<2 mm) through **lapilli** (2-64 mm) to **blocks and bombs** (>64 mm), with frothy **pumice** and dense **scoria** as characteristic clasts. The two great killers are the **pyroclastic density current** — the **nuée ardente** that destroyed **Saint-Pierre** in 1902 and buried **Pompeii** in 79 AD — and the **lahar**, the mudflow that destroyed **Armero** below **Nevado del Ruiz** in 1985.

Between fragmentation and fallout stands the **eruption column**, with its **gas-thrust**, **convective**, and **umbrella** regions. Its height grows only as the fourth root of intensity, $H \approx 0.22\,\dot{Q}^{1/4}$, and its most dangerous behavior is **column collapse**, which converts a stratosphere-reaching plume into ground-hugging PDCs.

Three ideas carry forward. First, **products are evidence**: a geologist reads grain size, sorting, and deposit geometry to reconstruct an eruption that no one witnessed. Second, **the same physics that builds a column can kill**: collapse is a knife-edge set by eruption rate and gas content. Third, **secondary products dominate risk**: lahars and ashfall reach communities far beyond the blast zone, and small eruptions can be deadly when these processes line up against a populated valley. With the catalog of eruptions and their products in hand, the next lesson turns to the practical heart of the field — the **hazards** these products pose and the **monitoring** networks (seismicity, ground deformation by InSAR and GPS, and gas geochemistry) that scientists use to anticipate them and to set **alert levels** that save lives.
